'''Helen Miriam Berman''' is an American chemist who is a Distinguished Professor of Quantitative and Computational Biology at the [[USC Dornsife]] College of Letters, Arts and Sciences. She is also a Board of Governors Professor Emerita of Chemistry and Chemical Biology at [[Rutgers University]] and a former director of the RCSB Protein Data Bank (one of the member organizations of the [[Worldwide Protein Data Bank]]). A structural biologist, her work includes structural analysis of protein-nucleic acid complexes, and the role of water in molecular interactions. She is also the founder and director of the Nucleic Acid Database, and led the Protein Structure Initiative Structural Genomics Knowledgebase.<ref name=googlescholar>{{GoogleScholar|dCWcLaUAAAAJ}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Demasters |first=Karen |title=A Bank Where the Currency Is Molecules |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 26, 2000 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/11/26/nyregion/on-the-map-a-bank-where-the-currency-is-molecules.html |access-date=October 22, 2008}}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20100703220527/http://sciencewomen.rutgers.edu/profiles/index.php?q=myStory&id=275 Helen Berman's story] from Rutgers University Office for the Promotion of Women in Science, Engineering, and Mathematics</ref> She is a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences.

==Background and education==
{{BLP sources section|date=May 2021}}
Berman was born in Chicago, Illinois, and grew up in Brooklyn, New York. Her father, David Bernstein, was a physician and her mother, Dorothy Bernstein (née Skupsky), managed her father's office practice. Inspired by her hard-working and scholarly father, she was interested in science as a young girl and planned to become a scientist or doctor. Her mother, who was strongly involved in the community and volunteer work, influenced her to be involved in community activities throughout her life.

During high school, Berman worked in [[Ingrith Johnson Deyrup-Olsen|Ingrith Deyrup]]'s laboratory at [[Barnard College]]. Deyrup encouraged Berman to attend Barnard as an undergraduate. While at college, she worked in a [[Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons]] laboratory with [[Barbara Low (biochemist)|Barbara Low]]. There, Berman learned about [[crystallography]], which would become a lifelong passion. She graduated from Barnard with an A.B. in chemistry in 1964.

Following college, Berman attended the [[University of Pittsburgh]] for graduate school, a place she selected because it was the only place in the country with a crystallography department, and one of the few where crystallography was offered as a subject. There she worked with George A. Jeffrey on carbohydrate structure, receiving her Ph.D. in 1967. Berman remained at the University of Pittsburgh for two more years as a [[postdoctoral research]] fellow.

==Career==

In 1969, Berman moved to the [[Fox Chase Cancer Center]] in Philadelphia, where she worked in [[Jenny P. Glusker]]'s laboratory before starting her own independent research program as a faculty member in 1973. At Fox Chase, Berman became interested in nucleic acid structures and in bioinformatics. She knew that logical organization of data would make it useful to a variety of scientists.{{Citation needed|date=December 2025}}

In June 1971, Berman attended a symposium at [[Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory]], where several scientists agreed that data on the expanding number of protein structures should be archived in a database.<ref>Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology, vol. XXXVI (1972)</ref> That meeting led to the creation of the Protein Data Bank (PDB) at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Bernstein FC, Koetzle TF, Williams GJ, Meyer EF, Brice MD, Rodgers JR, Kennard O, Shimanouchi T, Tasumi M |title=Protein Data Bank: a computer-based archival file for macromolecular structures |year=1977 |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=112 |issue=3 |pages=535–542 |doi=10.1016/S0022-2836(77)80200-3 |pmid=875032}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author= Berman H |doi=10.1107/S0108767307035623 |title=The Protein Data Bank: a historical perspective |year=2008 |journal=Acta Crystallographica A |volume=64 |pmid=18156675 |issue=Pt 1 |pages=88–95|bibcode=2008AcCrA..64...88B |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 1989, Berman moved to Rutgers and in 1992, along with other scientists, she co-founded the Nucleic Acid Database (NDB) to collect and disseminate information about nucleic acid structure.<ref>[http://ndbserver.rutgers.edu/about_ndb/index.html About the Nucleic Acid Database] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080920033203/http://ndbserver.rutgers.edu/about_ndb/index.html |date=2008-09-20 }}</ref> At Rutgers, she continued to study nucleic acids, their interactions with proteins,<ref name=Benoff>{{cite journal | last1 = Benoff |first1=B. |last2=Yang |first2=H. |last3=Lawson |first3=C. L. |last4=Parkinson |first4=G. |last5=Liu |first5=J. |last6=Blatter |first6=E. |last7=Ebright |first7=Y. W. |last8=Berman |first8=H. M. |last9=Ebright |first9=R. H. |name-list-style=vanc| year = 2002 | title = Structural basis of transcription activation: The CAP-αCTD-DNA complex | journal = Science | volume = 297 | issue = 5586| pages = 1562–1566 | doi=10.1126/science.1076376 | pmid=12202833|bibcode=2002Sci...297.1562B |s2cid=17422837 }}</ref> and also researched the structure of [[collagen]] in collaboration with Barbara Brodsky and Jordi Bella.<ref name=Bella>{{cite journal | last1 = Bella |first1=J |last2=Eaton |first2=M |last3=Brodsky |first3=B |last4=Berman |first4=HM|name-list-style=vanc | year = 1994 | title = Crystal and molecular structure of a collagen-like peptide at 1.9 Å resolution | journal = Science | volume = 266 | issue = 5182| pages = 75–81 | doi=10.1126/science.7695699 | pmid=7695699|bibcode=1994Sci...266...75B }}</ref> She is listed as a depositor on 38 structures in the PDB from 1992 to 2011, of protein/nucleic acid complexes and their components (e.g. 1RUN, 3SSX, 2B1B), collagen fragments (e.g. 1CGD, 1EI8), and other macromolecules.{{Citation needed|date=December 2025}}

In 1998, Berman and [[Philip Bourne]] together competed for and won the contract for the Protein Data Bank and the database moved from Brookhaven to the auspices of the Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics (RCSB), currently a collaboration between Rutgers and the University of California, San Diego. With colleagues, Berman redesigned the data management system, added new user tools, and made the database searchable.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Berman HM, Westbrook J, Feng J, Gilliland G, Bhat TN, Weissig H, Shindyalov IN, Bourne PE |title=The Protein Data Bank |year=2000 |journal=Nucleic Acids Research |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=235–242 |doi=10.1093/nar/28.1.235 |pmid=10592235 |pmc=102472}}</ref> Since 2003, the PDB archive has been managed by the [[worldwide Protein Data Bank]] (wwPDB), a partnership founded by Berman that consists of organizations that act as deposition, data processing and distribution centers for PDB data – the RCSB, the PDBe in Europe, and the PDBj in Japan.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Berman HM, Henrick K, Nakamura H |year=2003 |title=Announcing the worldwide Protein Data Bank |journal=Nature Structural Biology |volume=10 |pages=980 |doi=10.1038/nsb1203-980 |pmid=14634627 |issue=12|s2cid=2616817 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Berman served as the Director-Emerita of the PDB after serving as its Director (1998-2014).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-29 |title=Helen M. Berman {{!}} American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/helen-m-berman |access-date=2025-09-07 |website=www.amacad.org |language=en}}</ref> In 2006 the BioMagResData (BMRB) databank for [[Nuclear Magnetic Resonance]] (NMR) structures<ref>{{Cite journal

Markley JL |title=The worldwide Protein Data Bank (wwPDB): ensuring a single, uniform archive of PDB data |year=2007 |journal=Nucleic Acids Research |volume=35 |issue=Database issue |pages=D301–D303 |pmc=1669775 |pmid=17142228 |doi=10.1093/nar/gkl971 }}</ref> As of July, 2018, the NDB holds over 9600 nucleic acid structures and the PDB holds more than 142,000 macromolecular structures.

Also led by the RCSB, the [[Protein Structure Initiative]] (PSI) Structural Genomics Knowledgebase was launched in the Spring of 2008 to provide a continuously updated portal to research data and other resources from the PSI efforts.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Kouranov A, Xie L, de la Cruz J, Chen L, Westbrook J, Bourne PE, Berman HM |title=The RCSB PDB information portal for structural genomics |year=2006 |journal=Nucleic Acids Research |volume=34 |pages=D302–D305 |pmc=1347482 |pmid=16381872 |doi=10.1093/nar/gkj120 |issue=Database issue}}</ref>

Berman has also been active in the scientific community, serving as president of the American Crystallographic Association in 1988, advising both the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation, and serving on the editorial board of several journals. Berman was the executive producer and creator of the documentary series Target Zero which focuses on the medical as well as the social aspects of HIV treatment and prevention.<ref>{{cite web |title=Target Zero: Official Website |url=https://targetzerofilm.org/index.html |website=targetzerofilm.org |access-date=17 January 2021}}</ref> The three short films interweave real-life patient stories, interviews with leading doctors, medical providers and scientists; and state of the art molecular animations. These accounts illuminate the complex history of controlling the HIV epidemic and reveal the ongoing need for compassionate, patient-centered care and a true understanding on a cellular level the science behind the treatments.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Posatko |first1=Mary |title=Target Zero |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6297684/ |publisher=imdb.com |access-date=17 January 2021 |date=1 May 2017}}</ref>

==Personal life==
{{BLP sources section|date=May 2021}}
Berman has been married twice, to engineer Victor Berman in the 1960s, and to molecular biologist Peter Young from 1976 to 1999. From the second marriage she has a son, Jason Asher Young (born 1979), a physicist.

During the 1980s, Berman was diagnosed with breast cancer. The experience made her more focused in her life and her career, and interested in supporting other women who face the same diagnosis.
